descs.en: He blew open a shipping container expecting guns and found a princess. She won’t go home. She keeps coming back.

synopsis.title: Synopsis
synopsis.content:
Lee Jun Hyuk goes to West Basin at two in the morning to kill the man who signs the papers. He blows the lock on the wrong container, expecting guns, and finds five women who have been in the dark for two days. One of them is standing in the middle of the box, between the door and the others, with her hands open.

He gets them out, leaves them at a hospital, and won't give his name. Evangeline Lin finds him anyway: a noodle menu on a dashboard, three days at a corner table, two bowls ordered every time. She is the Lin family's quiet daughter, the paper twin, and she has been somebody's secret since she was three days old. He is a big, kind, talkative man who hunts the people who move people, and he has a rule about everything.

She follows all of his rules except one. She keeps coming back.

authorNote.title: Author Note
authorNote.content:
Evangeline says almost nothing in Every Flower in the Shop. I always wanted to know what she'd say if somebody waited long enough, and the answer turned out to be: not much, and every word of it on purpose. So I gave her the man who talks more than anyone in the series. He talks to frightened people so they'll follow his voice. She's the first person who ever listened to all of it.

It's a dark book in places. He's done terrible things for what he thinks are good reasons, and the book doesn't pretend otherwise. But it's mostly about small things done in dangerous rooms: towels folded in thirds, a lamp left on, a window box behind bulletproof glass, a man practising a woman's name in the shower. And about what happens when the one person who never asks for anything finally asks.

He's rich, by the way. Very. He just never had anyone to spend it on. That changes in chapter fourteen, and then it really changes.

contentWarn.title: Content Warning
contentWarn.content:
21+ · For adult readers. Mature themes and heated love scenes.

This is a dark romance with a lot of tenderness in it, but it has hard moments:

• Human trafficking: women held in a shipping container, and a lorry where eleven women died (The Container Had a Princess in It, Don't Stop Moving, She Asks Nothing, Someone Else Finishes It)

• Killings by the hero, mostly off the page (Don't Stop Moving, He Goes Hunting)

• An infected knife wound and a high fever, treated at home (The Night He Had a Fever)

• A dying man and morphine (The Target Is a Judge)

• A photograph of a captive sold online (The Traffickers Remember Her)

• A knife held to a father's throat, with no harm done (Jun Hyuk Meets His Father-in-Law (Badly))

• An abduction attempt, a head injury and a shooting (The Abduction Attempt, She Shoots First, After)

• A man found in a refrigerated container (Jun Hyuk Takes a Job He Hates)

• A sniper's choice on a riverbank (He Goes Anyway — Then Turns Back)

• A mother's death in an aid station, remembered by a child (The Borderland Boy)

• Grief for a parent the heroine never knew (A Letter From a Palace, The Throne Lets Her Go)

glossary.title: Names & Terms
glossary.content:
West Basin — The container terminal where it starts. Row K, the old control tower.
Nam's Noodles — Eleven tables on River Bridge Road in the border town. Phones go in a jar between the chilli oil and the soy sauce.
The karaoke flat — Two rooms over a karaoke bar that closed in 2019. Painted windows, three locks, a camp bed.
The menu — Nam's takeaway menu, taped inside the door, with his rules on the back (and two of hers).
The textile building — Eight storeys by the harbour. He owns it. Sixth floor: five windows of glass you can shoot at all day.
The window box — A steel greenhouse bolted to a twenty-centimetre ledge, behind a hatch cut into bulletproof glass.
The rabbit book — His school exercise book of names, boats and payments. There are ten in the end.
The Grey Lanterns — The border unit that took him in at eight. Old Ko's unit.
The court language — The language of the country she was born in, which is never named. She taught herself.
The heron — The gold crest on her baby blanket: a heron over three peaks.
No. 9 Fig Tree Lane — The house with a real address. Thirty-one windows, and every one of them opens.
The Open Door — The foundation she starts for people who come out of boxes.
Rule seven — Don't come back.
